front_blocks.md: Why does the C-X bond in a halogenoalkane have a partial positive charge on the carbon?

back_blocks.md: The halogen atom is more **electronegative** than carbon, so it draws electron density away from the C-X bond towards itself. This gives the carbon a partial positive charge (δ+) and the halogen a partial negative charge (δ-).

front_blocks.md: Reacting bromoethane with ethanolic ammonia under heat and pressure produces ethylamine and hydrobromic acid.

back_blocks.md: The NH<sub>3</sub> substitutes the Br in bromoethane via nucleophilic substitution, forming ethylamine (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>NH<sub>2</sub>) and hydrobromic acid (HBr) as the byproduct.

back_blocks.md: A **nucleophile** is an electron-pair donor that attacks electron-deficient (partial positive) atoms. The nitrogen lone pair in NH<sub>3</sub> acts as a nucleophile in the production of amines.

front_blocks.md: Why is an ethanolic solution of ammonia used rather than an aqueous solution to produce amines from halogenoalkanes?

back_blocks.md: Aqueous ammonia contains water, which can act as a nucleophile and cause **hydrolysis** of the halogenoalkane, producing an **alcohol** as a competing product. Using **ethanolic ammonia** removes water, ensuring NH<sub>3</sub> is the only nucleophile present and the reaction selectively produces the **amine**.
